events.title: The financial crisis intensifies
events.description: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy. Authorities support other financial firms as stress spreads.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon disaster
events.description: An offshore drilling explosion kills workers and leads to a major oil spill.

events.title: Japan is struck by an earthquake and tsunami
events.description: Coastal communities suffer devastating damage and begin a long recovery.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple more than tripled and Amazon nearly tripled, while Citigroup lost almost nine-tenths of its value. Bonds gained; the international share basket fell. The financial company’s losses at the start were a warning, but the size of its later decline was not written in the announcement.

The financial crisis intensified after the start. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in September 2008. Later came the Deepwater Horizon disaster and the earthquake and tsunami in Japan. Investors did not get to choose with those events already arranged on a finished timeline.

Citigroup’s loss is a reminder that a familiar name is not protection against financial trouble. A company can survive while an earlier shareholder loses most of an investment. At the same time, Apple and Amazon gained strongly. The result does not say every new gadget was a good bet or every bank a bad one. It shows how different the paths of individual companies can be within the same five years.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Citigroup changed leaders after mortgage losses. Kindle, driverless cars and distant planets offered very different kinds of news.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: A large, well-known financial institution could still suffer an enormous loss. A broad basket reduced reliance on one company, though it could also lose value.
reflection.what_faded_away: A change at the top did not instantly fix a bank’s problems. A new gadget did not make its maker’s future return certain.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew the exact recovery paths or losses. Company size and a familiar name were not substitutes for allowing for risk.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Amazon kept attracting shoppers and introduced the Kindle Fire tablet in 2011. Annual sales jumped 41% that year to $48 billion, but profit fell as the business expanded. It even reported a loss in the quarter ended September 2012. The shares still rose strongly, even though the much larger business had uneven earnings.

Mortgage and other investment losses helped push Citigroup to a $27.7 billion loss in 2008. Government support helped it survive, but the rescue and fundraising created billions of new shares in 2009. Each old share then represented a smaller piece of the bank. Citi returned to profit in 2010, yet that business recovery did not undo the huge damage to earlier shareholders.

Apple turned the iPhone into a major global business and introduced the iPad in 2010. In the quarter ended September 2012, iPhone sales were 58% higher than a year earlier. Apple earned $8.2 billion in profit that quarter and was paying a dividend. Its large stock gain was backed by a business selling far more products and earning far more money.
